title: Financial Statements of Not-for-Profit Organisations
outcomes: Explain what a not-for-profit organisation is and how its accounts differ from those of a business (surplus, deficit, capital fund).
Prepare a Receipts and Payments Account and state its limitations.
Prepare an Income and Expenditure Account on the accrual basis and distinguish it from a Receipts and Payments Account.
Decide the correct treatment of subscriptions, donations, legacies, entrance fees, life membership, endowments, special funds, sale of assets and honorarium.
Prepare the opening and closing Balance Sheet of an NPO and describe the special features of educational institutions.

meta.exam_tip: A 10–15 mark NPO question appears often. Marks are lost on classification (capital vs revenue) far more than on arithmetic — decide the treatment of every receipt before you draw up the accounts.

concepts.title: Not-for-profit organisations and their three statements
body: A not-for-profit organisation (NPO) — a club, a charitable hospital, a school trust, a library, a temple trust — exists to serve its members or society, not to earn returns for owners. Any surplus stays inside the organisation and is used for its objects; it is never distributed to members.

Instead of a trading and profit and loss account, an NPO prepares (1) a Receipts and Payments Account (a summary of cash and bank), (2) an Income and Expenditure Account (the accrual-based result of the year) and (3) a Balance Sheet.

Vocabulary changes: profit is called Surplus (income more than expenditure), loss is Deficit, and the owners' capital is the Capital Fund (also called the Accumulated Fund when members never contributed capital as such).

An NPO registered as a company under section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 must present its Income and Expenditure Account and Balance Sheet in the Schedule III format. The clubs and societies in exam questions are usually not companies, so the simpler two-sided format is used.
concepts.analogy: A housing society is like a family kitty: everyone pays in, the money is spent on common needs, and whatever is left over is kept for next year — nobody takes a "dividend".
concepts.work: CA firms audit thousands of trusts, societies and clubs. The first job is usually to turn the treasurer's cash summary into proper accrual accounts that donors, members and the tax department can rely on.

concepts.title: Receipts and Payments Account — the cash summary
body: It is a classified summary of the cash book for the year, without dates. It opens with the cash and bank balances at the start, shows every receipt on the debit side and every payment on the credit side, and closes with the cash and bank balances at the end.

Everything that passed through cash or bank is included — capital or revenue, and whether it belongs to last year, this year or next year. Non-cash items such as depreciation, outstanding expenses or accrued income are not included.
Its closing balance is normally a debit (cash in hand plus bank). A credit balance can appear only for a bank overdraft.

Limitations: it does not show the surplus or deficit, mixes capital and revenue items, ignores items not yet received or paid, and says nothing about assets and liabilities. It is adequate on its own only for a very small body whose only asset is cash and which carries nothing forward from one year to the next.
concepts.analogy: It is the passbook view of the year — it tells you how much money came and went, not whether the club actually did well.
concepts.work: Treasurers of small societies often hand over only a receipts and payments statement. A CA must not mistake its closing cash balance for the surplus — a large building donation sitting in the bank is not income.

concepts.title: Income and Expenditure Account — accrual result of the year
body: It is the NPO's version of the profit and loss account and is prepared on the accrual basis. Only revenue items of the current year appear: revenue expenses on the debit side, revenue incomes on the credit side.

Adjustments are made for outstanding and prepaid expenses and for income accrued or received in advance. Non-cash charges such as depreciation, and gains or losses on selling fixed assets, are included. Capital receipts and capital payments are left out.

Main incomes: subscriptions, general donations, entrance fees where treated as revenue, grants for running expenses, interest and dividends on general investments, sale of old newspapers, locker rent, hall hire.

Activity netting: income raised for a particular activity is set against that activity's cost — for example, tournament ticket sales are deducted from tournament expenses and only the net figure is shown.
There is no opening balance. The balancing figure is the surplus or deficit, which is added to (or deducted from) the capital fund in the balance sheet.
concepts.analogy: If the receipts and payments account is the bank passbook, the income and expenditure account is the honest report card: it counts what was earned and used this year, whether or not cash moved.
concepts.work: Grant-giving bodies and donors judge an NPO on its income and expenditure account — a society showing repeated deficits may lose recognition or funding.

concepts.title: Receipts and Payments vs Income and Expenditure
body: Both are prepared by NPOs, but they answer different questions: "how much cash moved?" versus "did the year produce a surplus?". Examiners regularly ask for the differences.

head: Basis
Receipts and Payments Account
Income and Expenditure Account

Like a profit and loss account (nominal account)

concepts.analogy: Same club, two cameras: one films the cash box, the other films the club's performance.
concepts.work: In practice you prepare the receipts and payments account first (it is the easiest to reconcile with the bank) and then build the income and expenditure account from it.

concepts.title: Subscriptions and consumable items — computing the year's figure
body: Subscription income for the year = subscriptions received − arrears of earlier years collected − advance for later years received + advance received last year for this year + amount still due for this year.

Outstanding subscriptions are an asset in the balance sheet; subscriptions received in advance are a liability. Old arrears that will never be collected are written off as an expense in the income and expenditure account.
The same logic applies to expenses: salary for the year = paid − last year's outstanding paid now + this year's outstanding − prepaid at year end + prepaid last year.

Consumable stocks (sports material, stationery, medicines, food): consumption = opening stock + purchases − closing stock. Purchases include credit purchases worked out from the creditors' account (paid to creditors − opening creditors + closing creditors).
concepts.analogy: A gym's membership: fees collected in March for April belong to April, and the member who has not yet paid for March still counts as March income.
concepts.work: Members' outstanding schedules are a key audit area — CAs check them against the membership register and question old arrears that should be written off.

concepts.title: Capital or revenue? Treatment of special receipts and payments
body: General donation (no purpose stated): revenue — credit to the I & E Account. Large donations without a stated purpose may be capitalised if the question says so.
Specific donation (for a building, books, a prize): capital — credited to a separate fund on the liabilities side, never to income.
Legacy (money left to the NPO under a deceased person's will): capital — added to the capital fund.

Entrance (admission) fees: if the question is silent, treat as capital and add to the capital fund. They are revenue only when they are small/normal or when the rules of the body say they are income — follow the question.

Life membership fees: capital, because they are paid once and are not recurring — added to the capital fund (or a life membership fund). Alternatives used only if the question says so: (i) hold the full amount in a fund until the member dies and then move it to the capital fund; (ii) transfer an amount equal to the annual subscription to income every year until exhausted, moving any balance to the capital fund on death; (iii) transfer an amount worked out on age and life expectancy each year.
Endowment donation: the donation itself is capital (kept intact); only the income it earns may be spent on the stated purpose.
Sale of old newspapers and periodicals: revenue income. Sale of an old fixed asset: the proceeds are a capital receipt; only the profit or loss on sale goes to the I & E Account.
Honorarium: a payment to a person who is not an employee (a visiting artist, an honorary secretary) for services — a revenue expense.
concepts.analogy: Ask: "Will this receipt come again next year in the normal course?" Subscriptions — yes (revenue). A one-time building donation or life membership — no (capital).
concepts.work: Misclassifying a capital donation as income inflates the surplus and can affect the income-tax exemption conditions of a charitable trust — a real audit risk.

concepts.title: Fund accounting — specific funds
body: A specific (special) fund is shown separately on the liabilities side: e.g. Building Fund, Prize Fund, Tournament Fund, Scholarship Fund.
Income earned on the fund's investments and fresh donations for that purpose are added to the fund; expenses on that purpose are deducted from the fund. They do not pass through the I & E Account.
If the purpose's expenses exceed the fund, the fund is closed and the excess is charged to the I & E Account (debit). The excess is not shown as an asset.

When an asset is bought out of a fund (e.g. a building from the Building Fund), the asset appears on the assets side; the fund stays on the liabilities side (or is transferred to the capital fund once the purpose is fulfilled, if the question says so).

Strictly, the word "Fund" fits amounts that are kept invested separately (Prize Fund, Scholarship Fund); where collections are not separately invested, the heading "Account" is more apt (Building Account, Tournament Account). A donated security or other asset is credited to the fund at its valuation.
concepts.analogy: A fund is a labelled envelope inside the club's safe. Money in the "prize" envelope can be spent only on prizes — and the interest earned on it goes back into the same envelope.
concepts.work: Donors increasingly demand utilisation certificates for restricted funds. Fund-wise accounting is what lets a CA certify that money was spent only on the purpose for which it was given.

concepts.title: From Receipts and Payments to I & E Account and Balance Sheet — the method
body: Step 1 — Opening capital fund: prepare an opening balance sheet; capital fund = opening assets (including accrued income, prepaid expenses, stocks) − opening liabilities (including outstanding expenses, income received in advance, specific funds).

Step 2 — Revenue items: for each income and expense, adjust the cash figure for opening and closing outstanding/advance/prepaid amounts and transfer the result to the I & E Account. Add depreciation, profit/loss on sale of assets, and consumption of stocks.

Step 3 — Capital items: take capital receipts (specific donations, legacies, entrance fees if capital, life membership) to the funds, and capital payments (purchase of assets, investments) to the asset accounts.

Step 4 — Balance sheet: capital fund (opening + capitalised receipts ± surplus/deficit), specific funds, current liabilities; fixed assets (opening + additions − sales − depreciation), investments, stocks, receivables, closing cash and bank (overdraft on the liabilities side).
concepts.analogy: You are re-sorting a shoebox of cash slips into three piles: "this year's running costs and income", "long-term things" and "what we own and owe today".
concepts.work: This is exactly the conversion a CA does for a society's annual general meeting: the members approve the I & E Account and Balance Sheet, not the cash summary.

concepts.title: Educational institutions
body: Most schools and colleges in India are run by societies registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860; in States with public trust laws (for example Maharashtra, under the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950) they are also registered as trusts. They follow the financial year.

Governance: office bearers (president, secretary, treasurer), an executive committee and a general body; each school or college run by the trust usually has a governing body that includes its principal or head.

Funds come from three main sources: (1) donations from the public (recurring or one-time, in cash or kind — land, buildings, securities, furniture); (2) fees — tuition, term, admission, laboratory and similar; (3) government grants — maintenance, equipment and building grants, and other special grants.

Laboratory and library deposits are refundable when the student leaves — they are liabilities, not income. Term fees are tracked in a separate account and spent on specified student activities (sports, magazine, medical inspection, library books, excursions, cultural events, examinations); any unspent balance is carried forward. Admission/capitation collections are regulated and in many places restricted.
concepts.analogy: A school's laboratory deposit is like a hotel room security deposit: you hold it, but it is not your money.
concepts.work: Auditors of school trusts check that grants are used as sanctioned and that refundable deposits are not quietly treated as income.

jobs.title: Turning a society treasurer's cash summary into final accounts
jobs.role: Audit assistant, CA firm (audit of a co-operative housing society's club)
jobs.situation: The treasurer has prepared only a receipts and payments statement and calls the ₹3.2 lakh increase in bank balance "this year's profit". Among the receipts are a ₹2 lakh donation for a new gym, ₹40,000 of next year's maintenance collected in advance, and sale proceeds of an old generator.
steps: Prepare the opening balance sheet from last year's audited accounts to fix the opening capital fund.
Move the gym donation to a Gym Fund (specific donation — capital).
Remove the advance maintenance from income and show it as a liability; add maintenance still due from members as an asset.
Take the generator's sale proceeds to the asset account; only the profit or loss on sale goes to the I & E Account.
Charge depreciation and outstanding expenses, then prepare the I & E Account and the balance sheet for the AGM.
jobs.takeaway: Growth in the bank balance is not the surplus. Accrual adjustments and capital/revenue separation can turn an apparent "profit" into a modest surplus or even a deficit.
jobs.think: The treasurer says, "The gym donation is our income — we received it this year." How do you respond?
jobs.answer: It is a specific donation given for a capital purpose, so it is credited to a Gym Fund on the liabilities side, not to income. Treating it as income would overstate the surplus.

jobs.title: Reviewing a school trust's accounts
jobs.role: Article assistant on the audit of an education society
jobs.situation: The school has shown laboratory deposits collected from new students (₹1.8 lakh) as income, and has spent part of a building grant on staff salaries.
steps: Reclassify laboratory deposits as a liability — they are refundable when students leave.
Trace the building grant to its sanction letter; spending it on salaries breaches its conditions and must be reported.
Check that term fees are kept in a separate account and spent only on permitted student activities, with any balance carried forward.
Prepare a note for management and the governing body listing the corrections.
jobs.takeaway: In educational institutions the question is not only "income or capital?" but also "whose money is this, and what may it be spent on?"
jobs.think: Why is a refundable library deposit not income even though the cash has been received?
jobs.answer: Because the institution must return it when the student leaves; it is an obligation (liability), not something earned.

mcqs.q: A Receipts and Payments Account is best described as:
options: A summary of the cash book for the period
An account prepared on the accrual basis
An account showing only revenue items
A statement of assets and liabilities
mcqs.explain: It summarises all cash and bank receipts and payments — capital or revenue, of any period — with opening and closing balances.

mcqs.q: Subscriptions received in 2025-26 ₹80,000 include ₹4,000 for 2024-25 and ₹2,500 for 2026-27. Subscriptions due for 2025-26 not yet received: ₹6,000. Subscriptions received in advance last year for 2025-26: ₹1,500. Income from subscriptions for 2025-26 is:
mcqs.explain: 80,000 − 4,000 − 2,500 + 6,000 + 1,500 = ₹81,000. A common slip is to forget last year's advance (₹79,500).

mcqs.q: A club receives entrance fees of ₹25,000. The question gives no instruction on their treatment. They should be:
options: Added to the capital fund
Credited to the I & E Account
Shown as a current liability
Deducted from subscriptions
mcqs.explain: When the question is silent, entrance fees are treated as a capital receipt and added to the capital fund.

mcqs.q: Sale of old newspapers by a library is shown as:
options: Income in the I & E Account
A capital receipt added to the capital fund
A deduction from the cost of books
A liability
mcqs.explain: It is a small recurring revenue receipt — credited to the I & E Account.

mcqs.q: An amount received by a charitable hospital under the will of a deceased donor is called:
options: A legacy, treated as capital
An honorarium, treated as revenue
A subscription, treated as revenue
An endowment expense
mcqs.explain: A legacy is a gift under a will; it is capitalised and added to the capital fund.

mcqs.q: On 1 April a club had: cash ₹12,000, furniture ₹90,000, subscriptions outstanding ₹8,000, outstanding salaries ₹5,000 and a Building Fund of ₹40,000. Its capital fund was:
mcqs.explain: Assets 1,10,000 − liabilities (5,000 + Building Fund 40,000) = ₹65,000. The Building Fund is a liability, not part of the capital fund.

mcqs.q: Opening stock of sports material ₹6,000; amount paid for sports material ₹42,000 (including ₹3,000 owed for last year); ₹2,500 is owed for this year's purchases; closing stock ₹7,500. Sports material consumed is:
A donation received specifically for building a hall is:
options: Credited to a Building Fund on the liabilities side
Credited to the I & E Account
Shown on the assets side
Deducted from the capital fund
mcqs.explain: Specific donations are capital and kept in a separate fund on the liabilities side.

mcqs.q: Tournament Fund ₹20,000; tournament expenses for the year ₹26,000. The excess of ₹6,000 will be:
options: Debited to the I & E Account
Shown as an asset in the balance sheet
Deducted from the capital fund directly without passing through I & E
Carried forward as a negative fund balance
mcqs.explain: Once a specific fund is exhausted, the excess expenditure is charged to the I & E Account; it is not an asset.

mcqs.q: Old furniture with a book value of ₹18,000 is sold for ₹15,000. In the I & E Account the club will show:
options: Loss on sale ₹3,000 on the debit side
Sale proceeds ₹15,000 on the credit side
Book value ₹18,000 on the debit side
Nothing — it is a capital item
mcqs.explain: Sale proceeds of a fixed asset are a capital receipt; only the profit or loss on sale goes to the I & E Account.

mcqs.q: Which of these does NOT appear in an Income and Expenditure Account?
options: Purchase of furniture
Depreciation on furniture
Outstanding salary for the year
Subscriptions due but not received
mcqs.explain: Purchase of furniture is capital expenditure — it goes to the balance sheet. The others are revenue items of the year.

mcqs.q: A token payment to a visiting expert who is not an employee of the NPO is called:
options: Honorarium
Legacy
Endowment
Subscription
mcqs.explain: An honorarium is paid for services by a non-employee — a revenue expense.

mcqs.q: An NPO registered under section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 prepares its Income and Expenditure Account and Balance Sheet:
options: In the format of Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013
Only as a Receipts and Payments Account
In any format the members choose
Only on the cash basis
mcqs.explain: Section 8 companies follow Schedule III; unregistered clubs and societies use the conventional format.

mcqs.q: Laboratory deposits collected from students by a college are shown as:
options: A liability
Income of the year
A capital fund addition
A reduction of laboratory expenses
mcqs.explain: They are refundable when the student leaves, so they are a liability.

questions.q:
City Public Library — balances on 1 April 2025: cash and bank ₹18,000; books ₹2,40,000; furniture ₹50,000; subscriptions outstanding ₹5,000; stock of stationery ₹2,000; rent outstanding ₹4,000.
Receipts and Payments for 2025-26 — Receipts: subscriptions ₹96,000 (including ₹5,000 for 2024-25 and ₹3,000 for 2026-27); entrance fees ₹8,000; donation for purchase of books ₹40,000; sale of old newspapers ₹1,800; fines from members ₹2,200; interest on savings account ₹1,500. Payments: rent ₹31,000; salaries ₹42,000; books purchased ₹55,000; stationery ₹4,500; newspapers and magazines ₹9,000; electricity ₹6,300.
Information: subscriptions of ₹7,000 for 2025-26 are still due; rent outstanding on 31 March 2026 is ₹3,000; stock of stationery on 31 March 2026 is ₹1,500; the library's rules treat entrance fees as revenue; depreciate books by 10% and furniture by 10% (on the closing book value before depreciation). Prepare the Income and Expenditure Account for the year ended 31 March 2026 and the Balance Sheet on that date.

Income
rows: By Entrance fees (revenue under the library's rules)
By Deficit — excess of expenditure over income

head: Liabilities

model.title: City Public Library — Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026
WN 2 — Key adjustments
model.text: Subscriptions ₹95,000; rent ₹30,000; stationery consumed ₹5,000; depreciation on books ₹29,500, on furniture ₹5,000. Closing cash and bank: 18,000 + 1,49,500 − 1,47,800 = ₹19,700. The book donation is a specific donation → Book Fund.

checks.label: Depreciation on books @10% on closing book value before depreciation

scheme.pt: Entrance fees as revenue (per rules); old newspapers, fines, interest as income
Book donation shown as Book Fund (not income)
Capital fund ₹2,92,700 after deducting deficit; outstanding rent and advance subscriptions as liabilities
Assets side: books, furniture, stationery, subscriptions outstanding, cash ₹19,700; totals agree ₹3,38,700

remarks: Most candidates computed subscriptions correctly but many forgot to deduct last year's outstanding rent paid this year.
A frequent error was crediting the donation for books to income, which turned the deficit into a surplus — examiners penalise this heavily.
Candidates who showed the opening capital fund as a separate working scored step marks even when the final balance sheet did not agree.
mistakes: Treating entrance fees as capital even though the question says the rules treat them as revenue.
Charging stationery purchased instead of stationery consumed.
Showing purchase of books in the I & E Account.

(a) Shanti Charitable Hospital: stock of medicines on 1 April 2025 ₹18,000 and on 31 March 2026 ₹22,000; creditors for medicines ₹9,000 (1 April 2025) and ₹12,500 (31 March 2026); paid to creditors for medicines ₹1,40,000; cash purchases of medicines ₹6,000. Find the medicines consumed to be charged to the I & E Account. (3 marks)
(b) The hospital's Tournament (sports day) Fund stood at ₹30,000; donations for sports day ₹12,000 were received and sports-day expenses were ₹47,000. Show the treatment. (2 marks)

Charging the entire ₹47,000 of sports-day expenses to income and leaving the fund untouched.

summary: NPOs prepare a Receipts and Payments Account (cash summary), an Income and Expenditure Account (accrual result) and a Balance Sheet.
Surplus = income > expenditure; Deficit = expenditure > income; Capital (Accumulated) Fund = assets − liabilities.
R & P includes capital and revenue items of any period; I & E includes only revenue items of the current period.
Opening capital fund comes from the opening balance sheet; the surplus is added to it, the deficit deducted.
Specific donations and special funds stay on the liabilities side; their income and expenses are dealt with inside the fund.
remember: Entrance fees: capital if the question is silent.
General donation and sale of old newspapers: revenue.
Sale of fixed asset: only profit/loss to I & E.
Consumption = opening stock + purchases − closing stock.
Excess of fund expenses over the fund → debit I & E.
traps: Don't treat the increase in cash as surplus.
Don't forget last year's advance subscription (it is this year's income).
Don't put a specific fund's investment income into the I & E Account.
Don't show refundable deposits as income.

viva.q: What is a Receipts and Payments Account, and what are its main features?
viva.model: It is a yearly, date-free summary of the cash book. It starts with the opening cash and bank balances, records all receipts on the debit side and all payments on the credit side, and ends with the closing cash and bank balances. It includes both capital and revenue items of past, current and future periods, follows the cash basis, and does not show the surplus or deficit.

viva.q: How does an Income and Expenditure Account differ from a Receipts and Payments Account?
viva.model: The Income and Expenditure Account is like a profit and loss account and is prepared on the accrual basis, while the Receipts and Payments Account is a cash summary on the cash basis. The income and expenditure account includes only revenue items of the current year, whether received or not, while receipts and payments includes capital and revenue items of any period. The income and expenditure account has no opening balance and its balance is the surplus or deficit, whereas receipts and payments starts and ends with cash and bank balances.

viva.q: How are entrance fees treated in the accounts of a club?
viva.model: Entrance fees are normally treated as a capital receipt and added to the capital fund, because they are not recurring and give the member no extra privilege. If the question is silent, we always capitalise them. They are treated as revenue and credited to the Income and Expenditure Account only when the amount is small or normal, or when the rules of the club say they are income.

viva.q: Distinguish between a general donation, a specific donation and a legacy, and state their treatment.
viva.model: A general donation is revenue income credited to the Income and Expenditure Account, because it is received without any stated purpose. A specific donation is capitalised in a separate fund on the liabilities side, because it is given for a particular purpose such as a building. A legacy is an amount received under the will of a deceased person; it is a capital receipt added to the capital fund.

viva.q: How are life membership fees treated? Mention the alternative methods.
viva.model: Life membership fees are a capital receipt because they are received only once and do not recur, so they are added to the capital fund or a life membership fund. Alternatively, if the rules say so, an amount equal to the annual subscription can be transferred to income every year until the amount is used up, the balance going to the capital fund when the member dies; or the whole amount can be held in a fund until the member dies; or an amount based on the age and life expectancy of the member can be transferred to income each year.

viva.q: Explain fund accounting. What happens when expenses on a specific fund exceed the fund?
viva.model: Under fund accounting, money received for a specific purpose is kept in a separate fund on the liabilities side, such as a prize fund or a building fund. Income from the fund's investments and fresh donations for the purpose are added to the fund, and expenses on that purpose are deducted from the fund, not charged to the Income and Expenditure Account. If the expenses exceed the fund, the fund is closed and the excess is debited to the Income and Expenditure Account; it is not shown as an asset.

cases.title: Lakeside Club — closing the books for 2025-26
cases.case: Lakeside Club started 2025-26 with cash ₹20,000, a clubhouse worth ₹3,00,000 and subscriptions outstanding of ₹8,000; it owed ₹3,000 for electricity. During the year it received subscriptions of ₹1,80,000 (of which ₹8,000 related to 2024-25 and ₹5,000 to 2026-27); ₹3,000 had been received in advance last year for 2025-26, and ₹10,000 is still due for 2025-26. It also received a donation of ₹1,00,000 for a swimming pool, entrance fees of ₹15,000 (no instruction given) and ₹24,000 from the sale of tickets for an inter-club match whose expenses were ₹30,000.
